items.title: Center for Anticipation 2.0: Human, Artificial Intelligence, and Domain Expert in the Study of Possible Futures
items.abstract: Center for Anticipation 2.0 is an independent research initiative founded by Sergey Antonovich Kravchenko, continuing the work of the original Center for Anticipation (2008–2018). The project investigates how possible futures are represented in human experience through dreams, intuition, premonitions, altered states of consciousness, and anticipatory processes. Particular attention is given to the transition from an initial subjective experience to interpretation, prospective formulation, independent verification, preparedness, and responsible action. The research framework combines phenomenological documentation, the Method of Significant Associations, temporal analysis, alternative explanatory models, and collaboration among human researchers, artificial intelligence, and domain experts. The project distinguishes ordinary psychological anticipation and unconscious inference from the more demanding hypothesis of precognition. The existence of an unusual subjective experience is not treated as evidence of information transfer from the future. All prospective claims require time-stamped documentation, clearly defined verification criteria, consideration of unsuccessful predictions, and independent assessment. The Center aims to develop transparent research protocols, a cumulative archive of documented observations, and opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration. This publication presents the conceptual and methodological foundations of Center for Anticipation 2.0 (Version 1.0, October 2026). The Russian and English texts are provided as two language versions of the same publication. Researchers in psychology, consciousness studies, philosophy of time, cognitive science, statistics, and artificial intelligence are invited to contribute critical discussion, methodological proposals, and collaborative research.

items.title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors. We ask what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations work against which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The evidence suggests that the structure of an error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy. False positives that the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse, sometimes even with a low initial error rate. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family. Its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have been tested against only one kind of error. We compile the findings into comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.

items.title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
items.abstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.

items.title: Clinical Effectiveness, Safety, and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Insulin Management Systems in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into insulin management through decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational platforms, and automated insulin delivery (AID) technologies. However, the clinical effectiveness and safety of AI-assisted insulin management remain uncertain. Objective: To systematically evaluate evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating AI-assisted insulin management systems in individuals with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for RCTs evaluating AI-enabled insulin management interventions in insulin-treated individuals with diabetes. Eligible studies compared AI-based systems with standard care, clinician-guided insulin titration, conventional bolus calculators, or other AID algorithms. Outcomes included glycemic control, insulin titration, safety, and implementation-related measures. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Results: We included seven RCTs published between 2020 and 2025. Interventions comprised clinical decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational AI platforms, neural-network-based artificial pancreas algorithms, and exercise-aware AID systems. AI-assisted interventions consistently demonstrated favorable safety profiles, with no increase in severe hypoglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or serious adverse events. Some systems, particularly fully automated closed-loop platforms and conversational AI-guided insulin titration, showed improvements in time in range, glucose control, adherence, and insulin optimization. User acceptance and adherence emerged as important determinants of effectiveness. Conclusions: Current randomized evidence suggests that AI-assisted insulin management systems are safe, feasible, and capable of achieving glycemic outcomes comparable to conventional care. Although certain technologies demonstrate promising clinical benefits, the evidence base remains limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up durations, and heterogeneity across interventions. Larger, long-term randomized trials are needed to establish comparative effectiveness, optimize human–AI interaction, and support broader clinical implementation.

items.title: Co-producing sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries on the MOSE megaproject: Media frames of continuity, stability and transformation in Venice
items.abstract: In Europe, sea level rise adaptation is strongly reliant on technological and engineering solutions. Megaprojects such as Venice’s mobile floodgate system MOSE are meant to provide protection to coastal areas. Due to their complexity and sizeable impact, however, megaprojects tend to be highly contentious. This article explores the interplay of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries in MOSE and how they build a collective past, present, and imagined future. Using data from Italian media, we identify frames that combine sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries that co-produce a legitimation of MOSE through techno-optimistic ideas of uniqueness and innovation, thereby illustrating how cultural and historical values shape spatial and sociotechnical imaginaries to construct the acceptance of wide-scale megaprojects. However, imaginaries of megaprojects also reveal contradictions: when ecological issues are framed as invasive events, imaginaries reject techno-optimism and place nature at the top of the hierarchy of space and place. Our study helps to deepen the conceptual understanding of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries by looking at how they intertwine with temporal and spatial-hierarchical dimensions.

items.title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learning signal is not grounded in criterion outcomes and can lead to reward degradation. This motivates us to reframe the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment, where privileged rubric information serves as a relevance cue for credit allocation rather than a source of imitation targets. Accordingly, we propose CoCA, which derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens based on criterion-induced distribution shifts, yielding both outcome-grounded and fine-grained learning signals. Empirically, CoCA achieves an average gain of +4.2% over standard rubric-based RL across medicine and science benchmarks, demonstrating more effective learning on open-ended tasks.

items.title: Cognitive workload across subjective and electrodermal measures in relation to previous-night sleep
items.abstract: Introduction Cognitive workload is commonly assessed using both subjective and physiological indicators, although these measures may reflect different aspects of task-related strain. Sleep duration may further modify perceived task demand without producing proportional changes in physiological activation. This study examined the association between perceived cognitive workload and electrodermal task reactivity, and explored whether previous-night short sleep was associated with higher subjective workload without increased electrodermal activation. Methods A total of 52 adults were initially assessed; two were excluded due to violation of predefined eligibility criteria, resulting in a final analytical sample of 50 participants. Participants reported previous-night sleep duration and subjective sleep quality, completed a 5-min resting baseline, and then performed the Determination Test from the Vienna Test System. Electrodermal activity was recorded continuously during baseline and task performance, while perceived workload was assessed after the task using the NASA Task Load Index. Task-related electrodermal reactivity was calculated as GSR task–baseline difference, and participants were classified into short-sleep (< 7 h) and normal-sleep (≥7 h) groups. Results NASA-TLX total workload was not significantly associated with GSR task–baseline difference (rho = 0.126, p = 0.383). In the uncorrected threshold-based comparison, participants with short sleep reported higher perceived workload than those with normal sleep (64.44 ± 8.31 vs. 58.70 ± 9.57; p = 0.027), whereas GSR task–baseline difference was nearly identical between groups (4.57 ± 2.19 vs. 4.61 ± 2.93 μS; p = 0.884). However, the workload difference did not survive FDR correction across exploratory subgroup comparisons and should therefore be interpreted as a nominal finding. Discussion Overall, perceived workload and electrodermal reactivity showed limited correspondence, whereas the sleep-related analyses did not provide consistent evidence of an association with either outcome.

items.title: Col-Ovo: Smartphone-based artificial intelligence for rapid counting of Aedes mosquito eggs under field conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Background The global expansion of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes has intensified the transmission of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses, increasing the need for scalable surveillance tools. OviCol, a low-cost ovitrap-based strategy integrating mosquito monitoring and control, has shown promise for community-based vector management. However, large-scale deployment generates thousands of oviposition substrates that require labor-intensive manual egg counting, creating a major operational bottleneck. This study aimed to develop and evaluate Col-Ovo, an artificial intelligence-based system for automated counting of Ae. aegypti eggs from smartphone images collected under routine field conditions. Methods Col-Ovo was developed using a YOLOv11m object-detection model trained on 275 oviposition substrates (20.5 cm strips) collected through operational surveillance activities. Images were captured in situ using smartphones without preprocessing and included samples stained with bioattractants (blackstrap molasses and Saccharomyces cerevisiae ) as well as sand and particulate debris. The system was designed to tolerate image compression generated by messaging platforms, such as WhatsApp. Performance was assessed by comparing automated egg counts with expert manual counts and virtual-human counts conducted through the OviLab platform using >200% image magnification. Agreement between methods was evaluated using correlation and concordance analyses. Results Col-Ovo successfully detected and quantified Ae. aegypti eggs under challenging field conditions, including heavily stained and debris-contaminated substrates. Col-Ovo showed strong agreement with human evaluators (Spearman ρ = 0.91; Lin’s ρc = 0.89; MAE = 22.1 eggs) and with OviLab counts, with no significant difference in paired comparisons ( P = 0.252). The system reduced processing time from approximately 15 min per substrate to less than 3 s, representing a substantial increase in operational efficiency. Performance remained robust when analyzing compressed smartphone images shared through common messaging applications. Conclusions Col-Ovo provides a rapid, accurate, and scalable approach for quantifying Ae. aegypti eggs from smartphone images. By eliminating the need for specialized equipment or image preprocessing, the system addresses a critical barrier to large-scale ovitrap surveillance. Integrated with the OviLab platform, Col-Ovo offers a flexible digital infrastructure that can strengthen vector surveillance, support timely public health responses, and facilitate the expansion of community-based mosquito control programs.

items.title: Collapse, Repair, and Drift: Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models
items.abstract: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is commonly monitored through training and evaluation loss, but loss does not fully characterize how model functionality evolves along the same trajectory. We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$. Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse, repair, and drift, and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation.
